If the same token (e.g., C1) appears multiple times, it consistently refers to the same class (C) or method (M) throughout the report. These tokens are not complete qualified names. Always confirm actual identifiers by inspecting the source code using get_code_snippet.

You will be given 9 opportunities to interact with functions to gather information for the debugging. An example diagnosis would look like follows.

Title: Diagnosis
Details: The corresponding issue report describes that tooltip text in the UI is displayed with HTML entities such as " instead of the intended characters. This strongly suggests a missing escaping or decoding step in tooltip generation. Inspecting the implementation of StandardToolTipTagFragmentGenerator.generateToolTipFragment reveals that it directly returns the toolTipText without applying any escaping. Recent issue reports mention similar encoding or escaping problems in related UI components, reinforcing the suspicion that this method lacks proper handling. The behavior observed in the code matches the issue report's symptoms, indicating that missing escaping in this method is the likely root cause.

After providing this diagnosis, you will be prompted to suggest which methods would be the best locations to be fixed. The answers should be in the form of `ClassName.MethodName(ArgType1, ArgType2, ...)` without commentary (one per line), as your answer will be automatically processed before finally being presented to the user.

messages.content:
Title: Diagnosis
Details: 
- What the test does
  - testMath828Cycle sets up a minimization LP with 31 variables, many “≥” constraints, and non-negativity, and calls SimplexSolver.optimize(...). The test expects the solver to complete without throwing UnboundedSolutionException (the intent of this test relates to MATH-828, i.e., preventing cycling/handling degeneracy).

- Observed failure
  - The solver throws UnboundedSolutionException during optimization.

- Relevant code path
  - SimplexSolver.doOptimize constructs the tableau, runs Phase 1, drops the Phase 1 objective, then iterates:
    - while (!tableau.isOptimal()) { doIteration(tableau); }
  - In doIteration:
    - It selects the entering column: pivotCol = getPivotColumn(tableau).
    - It selects the leaving row: pivotRow = getPivotRow(tableau, pivotCol).
    - If pivotRow == null, it throws UnboundedSolutionException.
  - getPivotColumn (lines 69–81) scans the objective row for the most negative reduced cost using a strict comparison against 0:
    - minValue initialized to 0, and it picks any entry where entry < minValue (no epsilon/ULP tolerance).
  - getPivotRow (lines 90–154) performs the minimum ratio test, but it only considers rows with a strictly positive pivot column entry using a tolerant check:
    - if (Precision.compareTo(entry, 0d, maxUlps) > 0) { ... }
    - If no such rows exist, it returns null (lines 113–115), which causes doIteration to throw UnboundedSolutionException (line 170).

- Why this fails here
  - With many variables and constraints (as in the test), floating-point round-off during tableau updates frequently produces tiny negative numbers in the objective row that should be considered 0 (e.g., -1e-16).
  - Because getPivotColumn intentionally does not use any tolerance, it will select such a tiny negative reduced cost as a pivot column (treating an almost-zero as negative and hence “improvable”).
  - Then getPivotRow applies a tolerant positivity check (Precision.compareTo > 0). If all entries in that pivot column are non-positive within tolerance (i.e., ≤ 0 up to maxUlps), no leaving row is found, and the method returns null.
  - This leads doIteration to conclude the problem is unbounded and throw UnboundedSolutionException.
  - In reality, the LP is not unbounded; the “improvement” indicated by the pivot column was a numerical artifact (a near-zero negative reduced cost). The root cause is the inconsistency between:
    - getPivotColumn: strict check with no tolerance (accepts tiny negatives as pivot candidates), and
    - getPivotRow: tolerant check for positivity (rejects tiny positives as eligible).
  - As the number of variables increases (as noted in the bug report), the chance of producing such near-zero numerical artifacts grows, explaining why small problems “almost” work while larger ones produce many unbounded exceptions.

- Relation to MATH-828
  - The code contains degeneracy handling and Bland’s rule for ties in getPivotRow. However, this logic only applies when there are multiple eligible rows with the same minimum ratio. Here, the failure occurs earlier because there are no eligible rows at all (due to tolerance), so the degeneracy prevention does not kick in. The issue is not cycling per se but a misclassification of near-zero reduced costs as strictly negative.

- Conclusion (root cause)
  - The solver may incorrectly throw UnboundedSolutionException due to a tolerance mismatch:
    - getPivotColumn uses a strict negative check without tolerance,
    - getPivotRow uses a tolerant positive check.
  - This can select an entering column with a spurious tiny negative reduced cost, for which there is no valid leaving row under the tolerance, leading to a false unbounded diagnosis.

Based on the available information, provide the signatures of the most likely culprit methods for the bug. Your answer will be processed automatically, so make sure to only answer with the accurate signatures of all likely culprits (in `ClassName.MethodName(ArgType1, ArgType2, ...)` format), without commentary (one per line).
